# Iteration 3 {.unnumbered}

In Iteration 2, you built your own dataset from the raw HOPV files and trained your Iteration 1 models on it. Those scores are your baseline.

In Iteration 3, you improve the baseline **one step at a time**: you replace the single train/test split with cross-validation, tune the hyperparameters, and measure how good your clusters are. At the end, you submit your models to the Kaggle competitions for the first time.

The work is still structured, but you make more of the decisions yourself.

## Classification

Evaluate the stability model with cross-validation and tune its hyperparameters.

Complete:

* [Classification](01_classification.ipynb)

## Regression

Do the same for the HOMO and LUMO models.

Complete:

* [Regression](02_regression.ipynb)

## Clustering

Choose the number of clusters with the elbow method and the silhouette score, compare K-Means with HDBSCAN, and look for clusters that help your supervised models.

Complete:

* [Clustering](03_clustering.ipynb)

## Your first submission

When you have finished the notebooks, submit your classification and regression models to the [Kaggle competitions](#the-kaggle-competitions) below.

To predict the Kaggle molecules, download the sample submissions from the **Data** tab of the competitions and put them in `data/003_kaggle_competition_data/` (Git ignores that folder). Every edition has new test molecules, so use the files of the edition you submit to. The files contain only SMILES: compute the molecular descriptors of these molecules the same way as in the [Data Preparation](../iteration-2/03_data_preparation.ipynb) notebook of Iteration 2, predict with your models, and replace the placeholder values in the sample submission with your predictions.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Expect a lower score
Expect your Kaggle score to be much worse than your cross-validation score; for stability possibly no better than the sample submission, which predicts `medium` for every molecule (macro-F1 about 0.22). That is not a bug in your code. Finding out why is where [Iteration 4](../iteration-4/index.qmd) starts.
:::

## The Kaggle competitions

There are two competitions, one per problem. A new edition of both opens every quarter, with new test molecules; the training data stays the same. The current edition is **2026 Q4**, open until 31 December 2026, 23:00 UTC (midnight in the Netherlands):

- **[OPV Molecule Stability 2026 Q4](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/opv-molecule-stability-2026-q4)** (classification): scored with the macro-averaged F1 score, so the classes `low`, `medium` and `high` count equally.
- **[OPV Molecule Energy Levels 2026 Q4](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/opv-molecule-energy-levels-2026-q4)** (regression): scored with the mean absolute error (MAE) over all `homo` and `lumo` predictions together, in eV. This is the average of the HOMO MAE and the LUMO MAE.

You need a free Kaggle account. Join a competition and accept its rules, download its sample submission from the **Data** tab, replace the placeholder values with your predictions and upload the file. Everyone competes individually, with up to 3 submissions per day. While a competition runs, the public leaderboard scores your submission on half of the test molecules (100 of the 200); the final ranking uses the other half. Don't over-tune to the public leaderboard: it is a small sample. After the deadline, the edition that just closed stays open for late submissions until the next one closes: they are scored, but not ranked.

You keep submitting in Iterations 4 to 6, as your models improve.
